strengths: The paper addresses an important computer-vision problem: distilling high-resolution datasets without bilevel optimization. Combining feature-prototype matching with per-class BatchNorm regularization provides a relatively simple synthesis pipeline.

Reported performance is strong at larger image budgets. Table 1 reports 57.6% ImageNet-1K accuracy at 50 images per class versus 53.5% for CDA, and 59.4% on Tiny-ImageNet versus 48.7%. Main results include variability across three runs.

Table 2 demonstrates useful transfer within the ResNet family: ImageNet data distilled using ResNet-18 achieve 61.3% and 62.2% accuracy when training ResNet-50 and ResNet-101, respectively, at 50 images per class.

Component ablations, regularization sweeps, and visual comparisons provide useful diagnostics. The manuscript appropriately credits its principal methodological dependencies and datasets, and acknowledges teacher dependence, computational overhead, and inherited dataset biases.
weaknesses: The central novelty is insufficiently established. With the stated squared Euclidean cost and freely optimized support weights, Equations (7)–(10) reduce to minimizing (1/n) sum_i min_j ||z_i-b_j||², the classical k-means/vector-quantization objective in teacher feature space. This equivalence is neither discussed nor evaluated through a matched k-means-prototype inversion baseline. It materially changes how the proposed barycenter contribution should be positioned.

The weighted distribution formulation is disconnected from the delivered training set. Algorithm 2 learns weights w*, but Algorithm 1 passes only prototype positions into synthesis and returns images without weights. No corresponding weighted sampling or student-training loss is described. Uniform training over the resulting images generally does not reproduce the weighted distribution optimized in Equation (7), leaving a substantive gap in the distribution-matching interpretation.

The optimization justification needs correction. The constant-Hessian argument in Section 4.2.2 applies with the transport plan fixed; it does not establish convexity of the optimized transport objective over support positions. Algorithm 2 also updates weights before reusing the previous transport plan for the position update, without explaining consistency with the new marginals. Zero weights are permitted despite subsequent division by those weights. These issues affect the algorithm's soundness and implementability.

The experiments provide limited attribution of the headline gains to barycenter matching. Holding cross-entropy and per-class BatchNorm fixed in Table 3, adding the barycenter loss changes accuracy by -0.1, +0.8, and +0.5 percentage points on ImageNette, Tiny-ImageNet, and ImageNet-1K. Furthermore, the stated baseline in Table 3 obtains 36.1% on ImageNet at 10 images per class, whereas Table 1 reports 21.3% for SRe2L. This substantial discrepancy requires explanation and comparisons under matched training protocols.

Table 4 does not adequately isolate Wasserstein versus MMD. Removing augmentations and FKD does not establish that feature extractors, BatchNorm regularization, and optimization settings are matched. For one image per class and an identical feature extractor, squared-Wasserstein minimization yields the class feature mean, which is also the optimum of linear-MMD mean matching. The reported 0.48% versus 5.77% therefore cannot by itself support the proposed geometric explanation for the difference.

Efficiency and reproducibility evidence remain incomplete. Table 6 measures only ImageNette at one image per class, where the optimal prototype is simply the class mean; this does not exercise transport between multiple learned support points. Larger-budget ImageNet timings and explicit accounting for preprocessing and relabeling are needed to substantiate the efficiency claims. Appendix E also leaves barycenter initialization, solver step sizes, and stopping criteria unspecified.
